summary: Describes Autokey, a security model for authenticating NTP servers to clients using public key cryptography. It is designed so servers can stay stateless and timekeeping stays accurate, which IPsec or standard PKI do not suit well. It covers requirements, design principles and the protocol specification. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you ask someone the time, you want to be sure it's really them answering. Autokey is a secret handshake that proves a time server is genuine.

questions: how does autokey authenticate ntp servers
what is a proventic ntp source
why not use ipsec for ntp
subtitle: How an NTP client can check that its time server is genuine, without making the server remember every client.

tldr.problem: NTP clients need to know that time really comes from the server they asked, but IPsec-style key agreement needs per-client state on servers, and signing every packet with public key cryptography would ruin timekeeping accuracy.
tldr.mechanism: Autokey combines public key certificates and signatures, used only occasionally, with a pre-computed chain of hashed session keys that authenticates each later packet cheaply. A short series of request and response exchanges carried in NTP extension fields sets it all up.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational. It documents the Autokey design as implemented in an NTPv4 software distribution, as a basis for future work and a reference for that release. It is updated by RFC 9748.

facts.label: Message digest sizes
facts.value: 128-bit or 160-bit, each with a 32-bit key ID

today: RFC 5906 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 9748, so read the two together. It has not been obsoleted. It records the Autokey design and the NTPv4 implementation it was based on, and the RFC itself says it is a basis for future work.

sections.title: Why NTP Needs Its Own Security Scheme
sections.content:
RFC 5906 describes Autokey, a security model for authenticating servers to clients in the Network Time Protocol (NTP) using public key cryptography. It is informational and describes the NTP extensions as implemented in an NTPv4 software distribution, to offer a basis for future work and a reference for that release.

The RFC argues that existing tools do not fit. Key agreement schemes such as those in RFC 4306, RFC 2412 and RFC 2522 need state variables for each association, which contradicts the remote procedure call paradigm where servers keep no state for a possibly large client population. A scheme that put a public key signature on every NTP packet would, according to the RFC, give unacceptably poor timekeeping performance.

There is also a circular dependency. Cryptographic keys are only valid for set time intervals, but those intervals can only be enforced when the machines are reliably synchronized, and that synchronization has to come from authenticated sources. The RFC calls a source proventic when every server on the path back to the primary servers has been authenticated, and notes that proventic does not by itself mean the time is correct.

The assumed attacker can intercept, remanufacture and replay packets, inject false time values, or clog servers and clients with packets that need expensive cryptography. Autokey aims to detect and discard packets that were not sent by the intended sender or were modified or replayed.
sections.eli5: Checking every single message with a big lock would make the clock slow, and making the server remember every visitor would be too much work. Autokey finds a lighter way to be sure.

sections.title: Autokey Cryptography and the Key List
sections.content:
Autokey uses message digests to detect modification, digital signatures to verify credentials, and public certificates to trace authority. Packets carry a message authentication code (MAC) made of a 32-bit key ID and a message digest. The key ID space is split at a pivot of 65536: symmetric key IDs are below it and live indefinitely, while Autokey key IDs are pseudo-random values at or above it and are expunged immediately after use.

An autokey is the MD5 hash of four fields: source address, destination address, key ID and cookie, giving a 128-bit value. An IPv4 autokey is hashed from four 32-bit words and an IPv6 one from ten.

The sender builds a key list. It starts from a random 32-bit seed at or above the pivot, hashes it to get an autokey, and takes the first 32 bits as the next key ID, repeating down the list. The list is terminated early if a key ID falls below the pivot or collides with an earlier one. The final key ID and its index (the autokey values) are signed once, and the list is then used in reverse order, so the first key used is the last one generated.

A receiver runs the autokey test on every packet: hashing the key ID it receives must eventually reach the signed final key ID within the signed number of steps. This lets later packets be authenticated with a few hashes instead of a signature. Each key expires one poll interval after its scheduled use.
sections.eli5: Imagine a chain of secret passwords where each one is made from the last. You hand over the end of the chain, signed, then reveal the passwords backwards one at a time. Anyone can check a new password by seeing that it leads to the signed one, but nobody can guess the next.

sections.title: Exchanges, Dances and Timestamps
sections.content:
Autokey runs as a series of request and response exchanges, each carried in an NTP extension field and completed in order: parameter (host name and status word), certificate, identity, cookie, autokey values, sign, and leapseconds. The sign and leapseconds exchanges happen only once the client has synchronized to a proventic source. Each completed exchange lights a bit in the client's association status word, such as CERT, VRFY, PROV, COOK, AUTO, SIGN and LEAP, and these bits ordinarily stay lit until a general reset.

NTP has three principal modes and each has its own Autokey sequence, called a dance. In the server dance, the server keeps no per-client state: it regenerates the cookie from the client and server addresses and a 32-bit random server seed whenever a client packet arrives. In the broadcast dance a client uses the server dance briefly at start-up, then verifies broadcasts by the autokey sequence. In the symmetric dance each peer builds its own key list from the same cookie, and if both peers send cookies at once the working cookie is the exclusive-or of the two values.

Every Autokey message carries a timestamp, the NTP seconds when it was created, and files carry a filestamp. An extension field with an old or duplicate timestamp is discarded before any signature is checked, which protects against clogging by replay. If the server refreshes its seed, the old cookie is invalid and the server answers with a crypto-NAK, which makes the client restart. If the client clock is stepped, all cryptographic and time values are purged and the dances restart.
sections.eli5: It is like a series of questions a visitor must answer in the right order before you let them in: who are you, show your ID, prove it, here is our secret word. Once all are done, you just wave them through.

sections.title: Secure Groups and Identity Schemes
sections.content:
An NTP secure group is a set of hosts with the same group name, assembled as a forest whose roots are trusted hosts (THs) at the lowest stratum. A trusted authority (TA) generates private identity keys for servers and public identity keys for clients. All host certificates are self-signed; a client asks its server to sign its certificate and caches the result, so each host can hand a full certificate trail ending at a trusted host to its own clients. Groups can overlap in hierarchies as long as certificate trails stay acyclic, and a host holding client keys for several groups can prove identity only in its own group.

A certificate trail alone does not protect against a man-in-the-middle, so Autokey adds identity schemes. The reference implementation has five: private certificate (PC), trusted certificate (TC), a modified Schnorr scheme called IFF, a modified Guillou-Quisquater scheme (GQ) and a modified Mu-Varadharajan scheme (MV). PC is used mainly for testing and TC provides no protection. IFF, GQ and MV use a challenge-response exchange: the client sends a nonce, the server replies with a result computed with its group key, and the client verifies it. The RFC describes MV as a true zero-knowledge proof.
sections.eli5: A club gives members a secret handshake. A new person shows the handshake and the doorkeeper can tell it is right without ever learning how the club makes the handshake.

sections.title: Autokey Messages
sections.content:
Autokey messages travel in NTP extension fields placed between the NTP header and the MAC. A packet may hold several responses but only one request. The Field Type byte is read as the version number, currently 2. The Code names the operation, the R bit marks a response and the E bit marks an error. The Length covers the whole field, including padding, and the minimum is 8 octets. The reference implementation discards any packet whose field length is more than 1024 octets.

The Timestamp and Filestamp carry the seconds part of an NTP timestamp. A signature and a nonzero timestamp are valid only when the signer is synchronized to a proventic source; otherwise the timestamp is zero. The signature covers the entire extension field.

The RFC lists codes 0 to 9: a no-operation crypto-ping, ASSOC, CERT, COOKIE, AUTO, LEAP, SIGN and the three identity messages IFF, GQ and MV. IANA added matching field types to the NTP Extensions Field Types registry, with a request, a response and an error response for each.
sections.eli5: Each message is a small envelope stuck onto the time packet. The envelope says what kind of note it is, whether it is a question or an answer, and carries a signed stamp showing when it was written.

sections.title: Security Analysis and Clogging
sections.content:
The RFC says the protocol has not been subjected to formal analysis and gives preliminary assertions. In client/server and symmetric dances the NTP on-wire protocol resists lost, duplicate and bogus packets, so a wiretapper cannot succeed, and a man-in-the-middle that could simulate a valid cookie still could not prove identity. The TC scheme is open to a man-in-the-middle building a bogus certificate trail, so PC, IFF, GQ or MV must be used to prevent that. The model also assumes a middleman cannot delay an intercepted packet; without that assumption a broadcast packet could be replaced undetected.

Signatures are computed only when data change: autokey values about once an hour when the key list is regenerated, and public values about once per day. Clogging remains possible. Replaying cookie requests at speed is hard to stop because the server retains no state. In broadcast mode, replayed responses are dropped by the timestamp check. The RFC also admits that replaying old or out-of-order messages before first synchronization can stop a dance or symmetric peers from ever completing, and notes TCP has a similar weakness.

The bootstrapping paradox, how to get proventic files before ever synchronizing to a proventic source, is resolved in principle by assuming stratum 1 servers are proventicated by external means.
sections.eli5: The authors say honestly that this lock is strong but not perfect: a determined troublemaker can still make the doorkeeper busy, though they cannot pretend to be the real time server.

fields.name: Field Type
fields.desc: Read as the Autokey version number, currently 2.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Whole extension field including padding; minimum 8 octets.

fields.name: Association ID
fields.desc: Client or server association ID, used to match responses.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: Seconds part of the signature time; zero if the signer is not synchronized to a proventic source.

fields.name: Filestamp
fields.desc: Seconds part of the creation time of the source file.

fields.name: Value Length
fields.desc: Length of the Value field that follows; a signature and padding follow it.

items.label: No-Operation
items.desc: Returns an empty response; a crypto-ping.

items.label: ASSOC
items.desc: Parameter exchange: host name and status word.

items.label: CERT
items.desc: Fetches a certificate by subject name.

items.label: COOKIE
items.desc: Fetches the server cookie, encrypted with the host public key.

items.label: AUTO
items.desc: Fetches the autokey values: final key ID and its index.

items.label: SIGN
items.desc: Asks the server to sign the client certificate.

items.label: IFF
items.desc: Identity challenge and response, Schnorr scheme.

items.label: GQ
items.desc: Identity challenge and response, Guillou-Quisquater scheme.

items.label: MV
items.desc: Identity challenge and response, Mu-Varadharajan scheme.
